utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the Registry staff, members of the Office of the Prosecutor, members of the Defence team; good morning, General Krstic. We're a bit late for reasons you are well aware of, but we hope that we will be able to make up for lost time. Therefore, pursuant to the provisions of Article 86, I give the floor now to Mr. Petrusic for his closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning; good morning to my learned friends opposite, representatives of the Registry. The Defence would like to bid good morning to the technical booth, as well as the interpreters. After 15 months of trial, the Defence will today and tomorrow present its closing arguments, which will consist of two parts. The first part will relate to factual matters, command responsibility as it is regulated by Article 7.3 and 7.1 of our Statute. And in the second part, my colleague Mr. Visnjic will address the legal qualifications of the crime of genocide with which General Krstic is charged in the indictment. At the outset, Mr. President, the Defence would like to begin from the most disputed fact, in our opinion, and that is the date from when General Krstic becomes Commander of the Drina Corps. General Krstic was appointed Commander of the Drina Corps by the decree of the President of Republika Srpska on the 14th of July, 1995. It says in the decree that he's appointed to this duty as of the 15th of July, 1995; OTP Exhibit 468. The same decree appoints, as Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, the hitherto Commander of the Birac Brigade, Colonel Andric. Both Krstic and Andric, at the time when they were appointed pursuant to this decree, were at Zepa, that is, in a combat operation that was being conducted in the Zepa area, safe area. And Krstic as the Chief of Staff, and Andric as the Commander of the Birac Brigade, were commanding some of the units taking part in that operation. In order to be able to assume their new duties, they had to either move from those locations or carry out a handover of duties, a pass-over of duties at the headquarters where the positions they were being appointed to are located. It is clearly visible from the decree on the appointment of General Krstic as Commander of the Drina Corps that the president of Republika Srpska at the time, Dr. Karadzic, as the only authorised official for the appointment of generals, issued a binding document which explicitly instructed General Krstic to take over duty as of the 15th of July, 1995. That date has to be taken, and it's the only way that it can be understood as the date, the earliest date when Krstic could have taken over duty or, rather, the earliest date when General Zivanovic could have handed over the duty of corps commander to his successor. That is the 15th of July, 1995, and it is a date before which the substitution could not have taken place. The Defence relies for this submission on the decree of the president of the republic, which refers to the rules of service of the army of Republika Srpska, that is, Article 106 and Article 369; OTP Exhibit 404, footnote 44. That Article reads that according to the law of the army of Republika Srpska, only the president of Republika Srpska, as the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, may promote, appoint, relocate, replace, or send into retirement officers from the rank of major-general upwards. It is quite clear that President Karadzic acted in accordance with the law, and it is also clear that both Major-General Zivanovic and Krstic have ranks that fit within this range. The Defence has called evidence before this Trial Chamber to show that the pass-over of duty is a process rather than a fact that takes place in one moment. General Radinovic testified that according to military doctrine, the process of handover and takeover of duty for a corps commander can last up to 30 days, and under extremely complex operative conditions, even longer. And one could certainly just say that that was the case with Colonel Andric, as Professor Radinovic testified, who took over his duty not before mid-August. Further, according to the testimony of Professor Radinovic, the former commander briefs the newly appointed commander regarding his duties, obligations, area of responsibility, documents, and everything else, and of course the members of the staff; in other words, everything that a commander position entails. If we take into consideration the fact that at the time of appointment Krstic was the commander of the Operative Group for Zepa and as such he was in command of the Zepa operation, then the fact has to be acknowledged that it was indispensable for the pass-over of duty for the necessary operational conditions to be in place. However, it should be noted, for the sake of truth, that Krstic was the Chief of Staff of the corps, a career officer with a relatively long career behind him. But also for the sake of truth it should be noted that Krstic, after taking over the duty of Chief of Staff in September 1994, went to another theatre of war outside the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps and that he returned to the Drina Corps area in November 1994; and that after having spent a month in that area of responsibility of the Drina Corps as Chief of Staff, he was wounded and he was absent until mid-May 1995. Therefore, from mid-May, General Krstic was de facto a member of the corps command as the Chief of Staff, and he was in that position in the relevant period we are discussing. Regardless of General Krstic's considerable experience as a staff officer, as an officer in general, the time he spent in the corps was not sufficient for him to familiarise himself with every minute detail, of the area of responsibility, the staff members, the documents, the confidential ones, the less confidential ones, the state secret documents, and everything else that such a command function entails. All these are reasons explaining that this pass-over of duty is not something that occurs at one particular moment in time but an extended process. The actual act of pass-over of duty is regulated in the Rules of Service in the army of Republika Srpska, actually in the documents and rules that were taken over from the rules of the former Yugoslavia, and this anyway applies to all the other rules as well. According to those provisions, as testified by General Radinovic, the regiment, brigade, and division commanders take over and pass over duty before a ceremonious line-up of the unit in the presence of the Superior Commander. For higher levels of command, that is, the corps level that General Krstic belonged to and levels above the corps, the handover and takeover of duty takes place at a formal meeting which is attended by the subordinate brigade commanders, the commanders of other corps, and someone representing the Superior Command; in this particular case, it would have to be the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Upon the completion of such a pass-over ceremony, a report is compiled which constitutes an official document. According to the testimony of General Krstic, and also on the basis of other exhibits which we will be referring to, that ceremony, that meeting was held on the 20th of July, 1995. True enough, General Krstic says the 20th or the 21st of July. Simply, one can attribute this uncertainty to the passage of time, uncertainty regarding the precise date. Professor Radinovic, in the Defence submission of the 28th of May and Exhibit D181/4, as well as the oral testimony of Professor Radinovic, in quoting Article 609 of the Rules of Service, he indicated how the legal provisions regulated this matter. This submission of the Defence is borne out by Exhibit 181/5. It can be noted in this document that the signatory is Major General Milenko Zivanovic. From the contents of the document, it is clear that he was the hitherto commander of the Drina Corps. The document is dated the 17th of July, 1995. This actually means that Major General Zivanovic was the commander who was, in effect, in command of the Drina Corps at the moment the document was compiled. If we were to carry out an analysis of this document and compare it with OTP Exhibit 467, dated the 14th of July, from which it is clear that General Zivanovic was the hitherto commander of the Drina Corps, the Defence submits that the only conclusion one can make is that if General Zivanovic was the commander, as shown by the Prosecution document, at the time this document was issued, and if that is the last moment until when his command authority applied, then he could not have been the hitherto commander on the 17th of July, 1995. However, the document dated the 17th of July, D181/5, shows clearly that he was the Drina Corps Commander on the 17th of July, 1995. The Prosecutor, however, rejects even the 14th of July as the day when, according to this document, General Zivanovic is described the hitherto commander. Of course, the Defence has a different opinion. Furthermore, this document, that is, 181/5, confirms that the pass-over of duty took place on the 20th of July, 1995, because General Zivanovic himself states in this document that his send-off will be organised on that day in the Jela Motel at Han Kram. Analysing the word Dosadasnj, that is, "hitherto," a term that has been officially analysed by the head of the translation service in this Tribunal, it is to be found on page 8356 of the LiveNote of the 11th of December, 2000, the concept Dosadasnj is clearly defined and described, that is, the English equivalent "hitherto." In the submission of the Defence, there can be no doubt that on the occasion of the pass-over of duty, a report or minutes were compiled. And the Defence expected, at the beginning of this trial, in fact, we were quite certain that we would be able to gain possession of that report in the archives either of the Supreme Command of the Drina Corps or in the archives of one of the subordinate units. One could not have assumed that such a document could not be found and that wherever we looked for that document, all the doors were closed, which provoked a great deal of suspicion and doubt with the Defence. The Prosecutor - and I do not wish to interfere in their method of work, I would not like to be misunderstood - conducted an investigation into Srebrenica and was in a far better position, either through SFOR or thanks to the willingness of the Defence Ministry and the army of Republika Srpska, to gain possession of such a document. However, allow me to observe that suddenly General Zivanovic reemerged on the 23rd of April, 2001, and the notification, his document, somehow emerged out of the blue, and the Defence wonders how to explain the submission of that document all of a sudden, which again is not the kind of document that can be called a report on the pass-over of duty, a document over which there could have been no dispute. Naturally, may I make myself quite clear, the Defence has no doubts at all with respect to the professional activities of the Prosecution. Our doubts refer to the former Commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic. The Prosecution fails to take into consideration two undisputable facts with respect to the date when General Krstic took over his functions as Commander of the Drina Corps. In the decree on the appointment, the President of Republika Srpska, who is authorised to appoint and discharge generals, it states that the 15th of July, the day when Krstic can take over his duties as corps commander at the earliest moment, before that date, nobody could have done this. Nobody had authority to do this. It is the position of the Prosecution, as has been said, that it was the 13th of July, 1995. If it is, therefore, the submission of the Prosecution, which refers to the information issued to subordinate units by Colonel Jovicic, and it is Exhibit 905, OTP Exhibit 905, the Defence then raises a number of questions. And in providing the answers to those questions, it disavows this act, rejects it as a valid document on the basis of which the pass-over of duty is conducted. From this document, it is a notorious fact that on that particular day, there was no decree by the president of the republic. It was not in existence at all. And then the question arises, how can an officer in charge of personnel duties, who by nature of his job, should refer to the normative acts and regulations, legal ones and bylaws, can refer and rely on a decree which is non-existent as yet, a document which does not exist? Colonel Jovicic -- furthermore, this act as a piece of information, sends to the subordinate units of the Drina Corps, although Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there is no need to inform them, because according to Rule 609 of the rules of service, Article 609 of the rules of service of the armed forces, subordinate commanders, that is to say the commanders of subordinate units are duty-bound to attend the ceremony of pass-over of duty itself. This act, this document should be sent to the Supreme Command, the president of the republic, who must have knowledge of the fact of whether his decree is being implemented or not, because the decree is an imperative, normative requirement, a binding one in the legal system of the then-SFRY, and by the same token, Republika Srpska. Therefore, the President of the Republic, as the Supreme Commander, is the first person who most needs to be informed about the appointment on the basis of the decree. This cannot be seen in this informative document, and that is impossible. It would be impossible because the decree to which Jovicic refers, Colonel Jovicic refers, was never compiled. It does not exist. Furthermore, had the handover and takeover of duty taken place on the 13th of July, as is said in this informative document, pursuant to it, we would have the following situation: Colonel Svetozar Andric, who was appointed as Chief of Staff, simultaneously would be the Commander of the Birac Brigade, and that quite simply is not possible. It would be a duality of functions, and dual function is something which is inconceivable. Only the chief of staff of a corps can perform the simultaneous function of deputy corps commander, but we will speak at greater length later on, when he came over to take his duty as deputy and commander. Therefore, this would quite obviously have been duality in the functioning of the command system of the Drina Corps. Document 181/5. It is the submission of the Prosecution that on the 13th of July, the pass-over of duty took place, when the decree, as a legal basis, was non-existent. This submission and thesis, amongst others, they're justified by the wartime circumstances that prevailed. We feel that this thesis is untenable. In practice, of course, it is possible under wartime conditions that some less important regulations and rules of service are not always respected because of the prevailing situation and circumstances, and this has been borne out many times by witnesses here, and Defence Witness DB told us that too. However, in the case in point, we are not dealing with an unimportant rule. We are not talking about the pass-over of duty of a company commander, for instance, which might have, say, 150 men in it; we are not talking about the pass-over of duty of a platoon commander either. What we are dealing with is the handover and takeover of duty of a corps, which can number up to as many as 20.000 soldiers, so this is the largest formation in the army. Apart from that, not only are we talking about adherence to norms, but under given circumstances, there was no need for the pass-over to take place in the way as has been put forward in the submission of the Prosecution. In case there are extraordinary circumstances, like an offensive or other active-combat operations, the corps commander, for objective reasons, and these can be sudden disease or death, serious wounding, disappearance, if he is prevented from fulfilling his duties because of any of these situations, the chief of staff, who is at the same time the deputy commander, when the commander is unable to be present, takes over those duties and responsibilities. Therefore, it was absolutely unnecessary to violate any rules and regulations and to appoint an ad hoc corps commander. In our concrete case, all the more so, as none of the stipulated circumstances were fulfilled. There was no sickness, the hitherto commander was not prevented from attending. Quite the contrary. General Zivanovic was present all the time. He was in the area of responsibility. He took part in the operation itself from the 9th of July and onwards, quite certainly up until the 20th of July, because he himself, in document 181/5, says that on the 20th of July, he will organise a send-off and be present. According to the Rules of Service, this is a ceremony at which the actual handover and takeover of duty is conducted. Furthermore, in interpreting this document and linking it up with the Prosecution's submission that the handover took place on the 13th of July, one would arrive at the conclusion that in fact two ceremonies of pass-over had taken place; one, in the submission of my learned colleague of the Prosecution, Mr. Harmon, on the 13th of July, when allegedly Mladic performed this act at the command headquarters of the corps in Vlasenica; and another one, when Zivanovic himself informed his subordinates on the 17th of July that a ceremony would be held on the 20th of July. If that was, indeed, on the 13th of July, why then would this pass-over ceremony be repeated and staged again on the 20th of July? Is it, as seems to be the prevalent submission, a banquet of some kind or that kind of ceremony? Zivanovic, for all intents and purposes, would not have used all his prerogatives as Corps Commander and, in that capacity, informed subordinate units of the fact. Would anybody, on the 17th of July -- would it enter into anybody's head on the 17th of July - while in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade there was a whole collapse in the system, and judging by the reports coming in, the threat of Zvornik falling was imminent, that was taking place on the one hand; and on the other, a part of the forces were engaged in military operations towards Zepa - so would it have entered anybody's mind, given the prevailing circumstances, to choose that particular time frame to organise a luncheon, a banquet? Or if it had an entertainment character. Some of the testimonies that said that this was sort of an entertainment. We heard submissions put forward and suggested in that way. However, the Defence submits that that was not the kind of ceremony it was, that it was the official handover and takeover ceremony at which the most serious question related to the corps was being resolved, that is to say, the actual commanding of the corps. And those whose duty it was to implement the decree of the President of the Republic were duty-bound to execute it and decided that that would take place on the 20th of July, regardless of the prevailing circumstances. I say "regardless of the circumstances" because it is with this document on the pass-over of duty that the situation of command is regulated in the corps de facto and de jure. The other pertinent fact which throws quite different light on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pass-over of duty of the commander of the Drina Corps is the sojourn of General Krstic at Zepa in his role as Commander of the armed forces engaged in the operation which was code named Stupcanica 95 at the time. We must bear in mind the following in this regard: Krstic was in Zepa and not in Vlasenica at the corps command headquarters there. Apart from that, at a meeting held in the Bratunac Brigade, on the 11th of July, in the evening, General Mladic orders General Krstic that the same forces that took part in the Srebrenica operation should be prepared to take part in the Zepa operation. If Krstic was to have been appointed the commander on the 13th of July, why then would Mladic send him to Zepa, and why then would Krstic remain at Zepa? It would be logical to expect that he would leave him at Vlasenica, at the command post, and designate another commanding officer to be commander of the forces at Zepa. However, General Krstic was designated to be the one to lead the forces towards Zepa. Furthermore, Krstic does not appear in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, which was in a highly serious situation, nor does he issue orders of any kind with respect to measures to deal with the situation in that zone of the brigade which, had he been the corps commander, this would have been a priority task of his. This thesis and submission put forward by the Defence is borne out by the combat report of the Zvornik Brigade, and it is OTP Exhibit 609, dated the 15th of July, 1995, signed by Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, the Brigade Commander. Vinko Pandurevic, on that particular morning, the morning of the 15th of July, returned from Zepa, and had Krstic been corps commander on the 15th of July, quite certainly this report would have been sent to Krstic at the forward command post, because Pandurevic knew that Krstic was at the Krivace forward command post at Zepa. But similarly, Pandurevic also knew that Krstic was commanding only the forces engaged at Zepa and, therefore, he sent his report to the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica. The report dated the 18th of July, OTP Exhibit 675, also of the Zvornik Brigade, is sent by Colonel Pandurevic to Vlasenica. Why to Vlasenica if indeed Krstic was the corps commander? Why not to the forward command post? Of course Colonel Pandurevic knew full well the status of General Krstic, and, therefore, did not inform him of the state of affairs in the area of responsibility but informed the command in Vlasenica. A similar report, OTP 614, also from the Zvornik Brigade, is sent to the command post of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica. The Prosecutor, furthermore, amongst all the documents and particularly on the basis of document OTP 536 and 537, as well as OTP 483, claims that Krstic was the Corps commander in the days when these reports are being sent out. In document OTP 483, which is an order to attack the Zepa enclave - it is dated the 13th of July - the units are enumerated which are to take part in those combat operations. Krstic himself was at a meeting on the 11th of July at the Bratunac Brigade in the evening at which Mladic designated him Commander of the operation, and he had to plan and implement it. In an order issued, and the document is OTP 463, General Krstic issues orders to those units who have been designated to take part in the Zepa operation. The order is that they search the terrain. And this could be a normal operation after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave and possible surprises which the 28th Division might have in store for the troops when the 28th Division was engaged in its withdrawal. Therefore, it is by this order that the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, which had become within the composition of the units to take part in the operation for Zepa, that is to say, the order of the 15th of July, that combat report, in that combat report Colonel Blagojevic, and this is OTP Exhibit 536, informs General Krstic at the forward command post, because he issued the order to search the terrain. However, Colonel Blagojevic also informed the command of the Drina Corps at the same time. Had General Krstic, on the 15th of July, been the Commander of the Drina Corps, Blagojevic would not have sent that piece of information, that report, both to the command headquarters in Vlasenica and to the forward command post at Zepa. Similarly, this is what happened with respect to document OTP 537 of the 15th of July, where Colonel Milanovic this time sends a report both to the forward command post and to the command headquarters in Vlasenica. The Defence, throughout this trial, challenged the relevance of the intercepts, intercepted conversations, because it deemed that they did not have the probative value on the basis of which one would be able, with any certainty, to make any decision, regardless of what that decision would be, to the advantage or to the detriment of the accused and without wishing to elaborate the reasons, we have provided, set them out in our motion to the Trial Chamber in writing. However, in addition to this fact, the Defence would like to submit, regardless of the general attitude and stand with respect to the intercepted conversations, to go into an analysis of OTP Exhibit 556. Assuming that this intercept is an accurate one, and it is taken from the communication Major Jokic had with General Zivanovic, one could conclude that General Zivanovic, on the 14th of July, was at the command post in Vlasenica. On line 3, after addressing Jokic and saying, "Go ahead," Zivanovic says, "Take this as an order. Take this to be an order," and that he should convey to Obrenovic, to tell Obrenovic what Obrenovic was supposed to do. It is quite obvious, in the submission of the Defence, on the 14th of July, at 2038 hours, when this conversation was allegedly intercepted, General Zivanovic issued an order. In another intercept, intercept OTP 555, the person who intercepted the conversation states in the heading that the conversation took place at 0910 hours, between the Commander of the Drina Corps, Milenko Zivanovic, and Major Jokic. However, the person doing the interception need not have known when the commanders were changed. What is important, however, is that Zivanovic, on the 14th of July, was at the command post at Vlasenica, that he was there, and that he was giving Jokic a set of instructions as to what he should do. Among others, because of the situation we can only assume was taking place in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility, Zivanovic says that all they would have to do is inform Mane, the centre of public security. The next conversation, OTP 364/1, was conducted at 20 hours, 56 minutes, between major -- between a major and General Zivanovic. The major says: "How can I find out where General Zivanovic is? Because I've been waiting here for him on his orders since 1700 hours." "He's here." And several lines further down, Zivanovic says to the major that they should read his conclusions, and the major says, "Yes, sir. Yes, I understand completely. And then we'll focus on things down there." It is clear, in the position of the Defence, from that conversation, at least as stated by a certain major as a correspondent in this conversation, a major subordinated to General Zivanovic, it is clear that General Zivanovic is issuing the orders, for if General Zivanovic at that time did not have any command authority, the major would not be waiting for him upon his orders, but he would be waiting for him as agreed. If Zivanovic has no command authority, why would he be telling the major to read his conclusions and why would the major, fully in line with a relationship between superior and subordinate, give the answer, "Yes, sir," or, "I understand"? In the opinion of the Defence, these intercepts also indicate that General Zivanovic was in command and was issuing orders to subordinate units. In the submission of the Defence, these intercepted conversations also negate the submission of the Prosecution that Zivanovic handed over command of the corps on the 13th of July. Also, the submission of the Prosecution that General Zivanovic handed over duty in the afternoon of the 13th of July cannot stand, in the submission of the Defence. Document OTP 462 leads to the following conclusion: Had the changeover taken place on the 13th of July, in the afternoon, in Vlasenica, and had General Krstic at that time, that is, in the afternoon and evening, been present in Vlasenica, why would have General Zivanovic sent this order to the forward command post, when he was personally with Krstic in Vlasenica? It should be noted that this order was issued pursuant to an order of the Supreme Command of the same date, that is, the 13th of July. The Prosecution is using this order as evidence to challenge the testimony of General Krstic, according to which he was not aware of the existence of prisoners of war. In paragraph 3 of this order, it is stated that the armed -- I mean the captured and disarmed troops should be accommodated appropriately and the appropriate command reported to immediately. This submission or this paragraph cannot be proof that Krstic knew of the existence of prisoners of war. From the quoted paragraph, it is clear that reference is made to instructions as to how to act in potential situations which existed at the time this order was issued. And it can also be seen that at that time, and according to this order, there were no prisoners of war. Zivanovic is not informing Krstic by this order that there are prisoners of war which need to be put in suitable buildings, but only how they should act should there be any prisoners of war. Therefore, the testimony of General Krstic that he was not aware of the existence of prisoners of war at that time was quite truthful, and this order does not prove the opposite as submitted by the Prosecution. On the 11th of July, 1995, General Krstic received orders from the commander of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic, to plan the Zepa operation. There is no written evidence of this, though we will come back to that a little later, but in his testimony, General Krstic and Witness DB shows clear that that order was issued to the Bratunac Brigade. The Defence has proven that, in the period from the 13th of July to the 2nd of August, General Krstic was at Zepa, and that he was in control and command of the forces carrying out that operation. Similarly, it can be accepted without dispute that to plan this operation, the necessary documents had to be compiled, the forward command post dislocated from Pribecevac to Zepa, military units had to be gathered, prepared, and reinforced for that operation, and for all this General Krstic and his staff needed a certain amount of time. This means that as early as the 12th of July, in the early morning, and from then on, General Krstic was directly involved with the Zepa operation, and as has been stated, he had to be engaged on the preparations of the operation and, as of the 14th of July, its actual execution. In the submission of the Defence, bearing in mind the fact that Krstic was in command of a part of the forces at Zepa, until the 20th of July, the command duties in the whole area of responsibility was held by General Zivanovic.

But before that break, since we are at the very heart of the matter, I have a question for you. We know that for the Krivaja 95 operation, there was an order of the Main Staff, that is, General Mladic; after that there was an order from the Drina Corps Commander General Zivanovic addressed to several units. Here there's no order. Do I understand that correctly? There are only oral orders, no written ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. At the meeting on the 11th of July which was held at the Bratunac Brigade in the evening, about 21 or 22 hours, an oral order was issued by General Mladic, the Commander of the Main Staff, that Krstic, with a part of the forces, should be dispatched to Zepa; and on the 13th of July, General Krstic prepared the order for combat operations on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But according to the rules, should there be a written order, or was it sufficient to have an oral order?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the rules of control and command, it is up to the commander to decide whether he will issue a written and an oral order. The commander has the authority to issue both a written and an oral order, at least that is what the Defence expert witness, General Radinovic, told us in his testimony. It seems to me that this way of issuing an order was not in any way challenged or contested in the course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But would it have been more normal to issue a written order?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot judge what would be normal. But practice shows that in the military system of the former JNA, oral orders were also accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. I suggest we now have a break. Would it be a good time for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We're going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Petrusic, you may continue your oral arguments. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In this part of its oral arguments, the Defence will focus on the norms and regulations governing the system of command in the army of Republika Srpska and the Drina Corps. The headquarters and staff of the Drina Corps consisted of departments and organs. The departments were departments for operative work and training, for intelligence, for personnel affairs, and the branches, the armoured and mechanised units, the units of so-called ABHO protection, that is, chemical and -- chemical warfare, engineers, artillery and rocket units, communication units, air defence units, and electronic reconnaissance units. In these departments -- these departments were headed by the chiefs of staff, who were at the same time the deputy corps commander, who was at the same time the deputy corps commander. In addition to the chief of staff in the Drina Corps command there were three assistant commanders, the assistant for morale, legal, and religious affairs; the assistant for security; and the assistant for logistics. These assistants had under their command, organs and bodies to carry out their main activities within their departments. Thus, for instance, the assistant commander for security had his officers or assistants and units of the military police. The assistant for logistics again had bodies and officers for each logistics service who develop their rear posts to provide logistic support such as quartermasters, technical, medical, veterinary, and other services. As the chief of staff is accountable to the corps commander, similarly, the assistant corps commanders from these three departments are also accountable to the corps commander. The role and responsibility of the assistant commander for security is a specific one with regard to the chief of staff and the other two assistant commanders, and this role is regulated by the rules, an excerpt of which is to be found in Exhibit D158. What makes the role of the assistant commander for security specific is a certain dual control and command function and the competence of this assistant within the system of command of the corps. The specific Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. role of the assistant commander for security, in relation to other assistants, is regulated in the rules of the Security Service. These rules, of course, have also been taken over from the army of the former SFRY. In addition to being accountable like the other assistants to the corps commander, the assistant for security has also his so-called functional command chain, a chain of command, according to which he is obliged to fit the Security Service of the corps within the Security Service of the Superior Command. At the same time, he's obliged to link the security service in subordinate units into a unified security service of his corps. Each assistant commander for security has a dual responsibility. He is accountable to his own commander and to the assistant for security of the Superior Command. This duality almost regularly resulted in the independent activity of the security department so that in fact there were two chains of command, operational command, which was headed by commanders of corps down the level to the lowest units, and a security system of command headed by the assistant for security in the highest level command, that is, in the Supreme Command. And this was a constant source of problems, and in the opinion of troop officers such as corps and brigade commanders, there were frequent irregularities. And there was an instance when the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, requested, as early as 1994, that the security organ in his brigade should be subordinated to him in every respect and not to the security organ in a higher level command. And this is also something that General Krstic testified about. There is no doubt that these problems existed in those days as well, because the Rules of Service of the security organs allowed it, and as will be borne out by all the events that occurred around Srebrenica in the period between the 13th and 17th of July, which shows that that is precisely how the security system functioned. It was almost the rule for the security system to function as a separate and independent chain of command and decision-making. For most of the activities within the framework of the security department, which are of a general nature and which are not directly linked to combat security of the corps, the operational control and command system was not informed. As I have already indicated, a certain degree of independence on the part of the assistant commander for security was contributed to by the Rules of Service; or to put it differently, the Rules of Service provided a basis for such conduct. In the event of confidential operations, the assistant for security had no obligation to inform the commander about them, but he was obliged to inform the assistant for security of the Superior Command, who was the person who could give him orders along those lines. The Defence has the impression that the Prosecution has not fully appreciated in the proceedings against General Krstic this specific nature of the security chain of command within the Drina Corps. That is why the Defence and General Radinovic, as an expert witness, have sought to fully explain this duality of control and command and these parallel chains that resulted from this. When we come to the crimes described in the indictment and which occurred in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps in July 1995, this duality of command certainly had a decisive impact on the nature of command competencies and command responsibilities of the senior officers of the Drina Corps, including General Krstic. It seems to me that General Radinovic, during his testimony, argued fully that a necessary logical consequence of this security chain of command was a situation in which the security system at all levels of command took decisions regarding prisoners of war and what should be done to them without informing the unit commanders about this, the commanders within whose areas of responsibilities these crimes were committed. The Defence will seek to prove, on the basis of certain indicators, that this security system even used paramilitary units which appeared ad hoc within the territory of the army of Republika Srpska and which were not part of the system and were not under the command, allow me to say, the commanders of the units belonging to the regular system of control and command. The chief of staff is, according to establishment and by his functions, responsible for the functioning of the corps staff. As the person who is, according to establishment, responsible for operational planning, the chief of staff has the authority to require from other assistant commanders information which will make it possible for him to plan combat operations in accordance with the concept of the commander. However, that does not necessarily mean a priori that the assistant commanders were, in any sense, subordinated to him. Only the staff officers are subordinated to the chief of staff, and they are the officer for operations and training, for communications, ABHO protection, air defence, which I have already listed at the beginning of this section. When analysing the command responsibility of General Krstic with a view to making him responsible for the acts which occurred in the area of responsibility of subordinated units and commands, the expert witnesses of the Prosecution and, above all, Mr. Butler, with all due respect for their professionalism and rank - I'm referring to Mr. Butler and his expert report - they raise General Krstic to a level which he, in fact, did not have and which, according to the rules of command in the army of Republika Srpska, he did not have. According to their understanding, the chief of staff is said to be superior to the whole Corps Command except for the commander, including the assistant commanders. Both Mr. Butler and General Dannatt, when making an organigramme of the corps staff, equates the staff with the command. So in so doing, they also place the chief of staff above the level of assistant commander. Through our expert witness General Radinovic, the Defence has sought to prove that there is a substantive difference between the understanding of the staff in the doctrines of West European armies, which General Dannatt relied upon when interpreting the structure of the staff and the position of the chief of staff, from the doctrine of control and command which was in force in the army of Republika Srpska. According to the latter doctrine, there is no direct command responsibility of the chief of staff over the assistant commander, but, rather, the chain of command going from the commander of the Drina Corps towards his assistants is the same and is based on the same model as towards the chief of staff. So it is an identical level of command responsibility from the commander towards all three assistant commanders and the chief of staff and vice versa. All three assistant commanders and the chief of staff have an identical level of accountability and responsibility towards the commander in the command. The chief of staff does not have a privileged position in any sense within the framework of the Corps Command as claimed by General Dannatt and Mr. Butler, and it would seem to me that their interpretation helped the Prosecution to construe the responsibility of General Krstic as chief of staff. Apart from being in charge of planning of combat operations and of his duty to communicate with other command bodies for that purpose, the chief of staff has no other command authority towards command organs outside the staff and its structures, nor towards subordinated units and commands. That kind of authority rests exclusively with the corps commander. That is his exclusive right, and it is, in the final analysis, that which distinguishes him from all the other members of the Corps Command or any other command regardless of the level. The Defence has the impression that the role of deputy commander also has not been sufficiently precisely defined within the whole structure of the system of command. It is true that General Krstic is the Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps, but the function of deputy commander was not the result of a position in the establishment, because no such position in the establishment exists, but the function of deputy stems from the function of chief of staff in the establishment. Therefore, the legislator has not provided for a special post of deputy commander in the establishment, probably believing that it was not necessary, for if it were a special post envisaged by establishment, the legislator would have regulated the competencies of that post in the rules as was done for all the other organs in the command and staff. The rules regarding competencies provide for the competencies of the corps commander. All those competencies apply also to his deputy, but only when he is de facto performing the role of Commander-in-Chief. This means that the chief of staff assumes the competencies of the commander only when the commander is unable to perform his duties when his deputy has to take them over. When it becomes quite clear that the commander is unable to perform his command duties or when he's authorised to perform that role by a document, only then does the deputy commander take over the control and command functions of the commander. In practice, this means that the only privilege of the chief of staff is that he automatically takes over command competencies and command responsibilities when the commander is unable to perform them. This also means that the legislator sought to make it clear from the beginning who has the right to command and control instead of the commander when he's unable to do so. The very fact that somebody holds the position of chief of staff does not give him any exclusive right of command if the commander is available and if he is capable of commanding. Only as, what I have said, he is unable to perform his duties does the chief of staff take over in the role of commander. The Defence submits that General Radislav Krstic took over duty on the 20th of July, 1995, and he is seeking to prove that throughout the period when he was chief of staff while the current commander was General Zivanovic, General Zivanovic was available for commanding, he was capable of commanding of the units of the Drina Corps. In brief, Mr. President, the Defence would now like to focus on the demilitarised zone or, rather, the demilitarisation of the safe area of Srebrenica. The Defence considers that one cannot speak about, nor raise to the level of proof proper, the decision of the assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was signed by Mr. Krajisnik and which was referred to in the closing argument by Mr. Harmon, that it was the strategic -- that Podrinje was the strategic interest of the VRS, or, rather, the abolishment of the border between Serbia and Republika Srpska. In this trial, during these proceedings, we did not present evidence of this kind before the Trial Chamber. However, as the Prosecution has referred to the matter, the Defence will present certain facts to refute that thesis. Perhaps Podrinje was the strategic interest of the Serbs, but it is quite obvious that Podrinje was also the strategic interest of the Muslims as well. Had that not been so, why, then, would the Serbs, in the autumn and winter of 1992 and 1993, in these regions, have experienced the greatest pogroms? Why would they have left Srebrenica if there was no strategic interest of the Muslims vis-a-vis that area? But whatever it was, the fact remains that from the beginning of the war in the region, that there were combat activities between the two warring parties. The UN Security Council, with its Resolution 189, proclaimed a safe area here as of the 16th of April, 1993, and those safe areas were Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. With the Additional Protocol of the Geneva Conventions, dated the 12th of August, 1994, Chapter 5, Places and Zones Under Special Protection, Article 60, precisely devised the fact that the areas placed under special protection regime must be demilitarised. The demilitarisation, according to Article 60, envisages the following: that for acts of hostility, no immobile military installations and institutions be used; that from those areas, all soldiers be evacuated as well as mobile weapons and others; that the authorities and the inhabitants must not undertake any hostile acts towards the other warring side or towards anybody in the enclave; that all activities must cease with respect to the military effort. It is also provided for that one party in the conflict will be alleviated of its responsibilities with respect to respecting the status of the safe area if the other side infringes upon the four points of the agreement and engages in material infringement. The decision of the UN Security Council meant an agreement between the Serbian side and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the agreement which was subsequently signed was signed by General Mladic, on behalf of the Supreme Command of the army of Republika Srpska, and General Sefer Halilovic, in the name of the BH army. The first agreement was signed in April 1993, the second agreement was signed on the 8th of May, 1993, and the two contractual parties agreed that any military or paramilitary units must withdraw from the demilitarised zone and must surrender its weapons, munition mines, explosives, and all other lethal weapons. The second point of that agreement stipulated as follows: "No fighter will be allowed to have in his possession weapons, munition, explosives, if he wishes to enter the demilitarised zone or finds himself in it. The only exceptions are the representatives of UNPROFOR." It was also provided that soldiers would not be allowed to enter the demilitarised zone or to spend any time in it. The Serb side behaved in conformity with the agreement. The same day that the agreement was signed, the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Manojlo Milovanovic, sent to the command of the Drina Corps an order, issued an order, which was wholly binding that everything should evolve in conformity with the agreement, without any violation of the stipulations of the agreement. In presenting its evidence during the trial, the Defence showed a number of documents that were adopted into evidence by this Trial Chamber, and the documents range from D28 to D71, from which it is clearly visible -- from which the following can be clearly deduced: that within the safe area, there was a military establishment, an armed one, which numbered, depending on the source, from between seven to ten members [as interpreted]. First of all, they were the 8th Operative Group and later on they became the 28th Division.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] That the members of the 8th Operative Group or, rather, the 28th Division were systematically armed by their superior commands, the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to which we have heard testimony by Generals Hadzihasanovic and Halilovic. Furthermore, the Muslim forces from the enclave around Srebrenica and Zepa stepped outside the enclave and went in depth into the territory under the control of the VRS and the Drina Corps, where they carried out sabotage and diversionary action and where they affected the same operations towards the civilian population as they did towards the members of the army. Furthermore, another characteristic of all this evidence and material is that the members of UNPROFOR did not prevent them in doing so, or we do not have certain proof about that. We do not have anything to show that they disarmed them either, which was one of their tasks and duties. Following orders that the command of the 8th Operative Group or 28th Division received from their commander in Tuzla, it was clear that it was their intention to inflict on the enemy a loss of manpower and to conjoin in the north and northwest, towards the units of the 2nd Corps of the BH army. And in June of 1995, this became an all-out offensive. So that on the one hand, the offensive was launched from the axis of Sarajevo, with the aim of deblocking Sarajevo and linking it up to Srebrenica and Zepa, and to draw away the forces of the Drina Corps units from the area; and on the other hand, from the axis and direction of the 2nd Corps, an attack on the Birac Brigade, once again with the intention of linking up with the enclaves or, rather, the enclaves with the territory that was under the command of the 2nd Corps. It has already been stated that Defence Exhibits D28 through to D71, including D90, D91, and D92, indicated the clear cut intention of the Muslim armed establishment and their synchronised action in order to link up the units of the 2nd Corps with the units of the 28th Division. On the other hand, the army of Republika Srpska and the Drina Corps, at this period of time and particularly in June 1995, was on the defensive, and the testimony of Mr. Butler testifies to this. The Muslims forces from the demilitarised zone reached the culmination of their operations towards the Drina Corps and in the depth of the Drina Corps, and this culmination was attained in June 1995. It came to a head. As an example, on the 26th of June, and this was -- evidence of this was provided, the Muslim units sent nine sabotage diversionary terrorist groups to behind the positions of the Drina Corps and set fire to the village of Visnjica. And in the combat report dated the 28th of June, the 285th Eastern Bosnian Light Brigade sent to the command of the 28th Division and the command of the 2nd Corps -- it states that these brigades in the rear of the Drina Corps had infiltrated nine terrorist groups who had killed 40 Chetniks. The term "Chetnik" was the term that Muslims referred to the Serb soldiers and civilians by. I don't need to state that this behaviour on the part of the Muslim army was in complete opposition to the agreement on demilitarisation and gave the army of Republika Srpska the legitimate right, in view of the fact that UNPROFOR failed to act, to prevent any further losses to its army and attacks on its civilian population outside the enclave. Now, briefly I should like to talk about the Krivaja 95 operation. This operation was effected by the auxiliary forces of the Drina Corps; Prosecution Exhibit OTP 427 and 428. And this was done between the 6th of July up until the 11th of July, 1995. We arrive at these facts when we compare documents OTP 427, the preparatory order, and 428, the order for active military engagement. Both documents are dated the 2nd of July. The first time that the officers from the command of the Drina Corps appeared on the scene was noted and recorded at around the 30th of June, and Mr. Butler testified about that, and it was in the area of Bratunac. A group of officers spent some time there, among them General Radislav Krstic. Regardless of whether this piece of information is correct or not, we can consider with certainty that that particular date, the 30th of June, was for a time when the process of planning for Krivaja 95 began. Until the order for the operation was issued, two days went by. With the issuance of the order, the planning process was completed at that level of command. The time that was left -- the time that remained for the implementation of the order for the corps commander was the 6th of July, and it is precisely that time where the subordinate commanders are given time to plan everything, to bring in the units, group the units, conduct additional reconnaissance, corrections of plans and decisions and things of that kind. So we can say that at the level of the corps, the planning of this operation could have lasted two days at the most. If we start out from the fact that according to military doctrine which was in force with the VRS, the process of planning combat action at the level of the corps is stipulated between five to seven days, we must conclude that Krivaja 95 was an operation which was planned speedily and as such was not planned in all its details as is otherwise provided for by the provisions of military doctrine. This impression that the operation was not sufficiently well thought out and the lack of time for its comprehensive planning, we're able to say that on the basis of the fact that the plan for this operation did not contain the series of operational acts and documents which would otherwise be necessary and must accompany an operation of this kind. When I talk about these documents, they are plans providing for all types of security, for the engineers, for intelligence, for security, plan of action for the artillery, for anti-aircraft defence, orders for each operational and supporting activity for which separate -- a separate plan is compiled and adopted. None of these plans and orders were discovered except for the preparatory order for active combat operations and the order for anti-aircraft defence, as well as a signals and communications plan. It is our assumption that other plans, combat documents, and so on and so forth were not compiled at all, because the corps command started out from -- the corps command decided that the operation should be conducted as soon as possible, that it was limited in scope and target and that for its implementation, these kinds of documents were not absolutely necessary, the kind that were otherwise provided for by military doctrine. If we compare the preparation time and the time for the planning of this operation at the level of the corps and the time that the corps command allowed for planning at lower levels, we see that the operation was planned at all levels in totality for four days. The substantive basic document on the basis of which Krivaja 95 operation was implemented was the order on active combat. The title of the document itself gives the same impression that I described a moment ago, that it is -- this order for active combat was of limited scope, and these combat operations for Srebrenica were not even called an operation. The term used was "Order for active combat or combat activities." Had the commander of the Drina Corps considered that it was combat action of an operative type and not a tactical type, in his order he would have called them attack operation, and then this document would bear the title of "Order for attack operations." Therefore, the commander envisaged that these were tactical tasks with a -- of limited scope and limited target. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It is clear from this order which forces were engaged, which units were used, and which units participated in carrying out this order. We may draw the conclusion that the planning and implementation of this operation was within the limits of a legitimate combat action. Its legitimacy is based on the fact that it was launched against enemy forces, military forces which had launched action against the Drina Corps forces that suffered heavy losses, and the Muslim forces, without any form of camouflage, went counter to the demilitarised zone agreement and the United Nations Resolution 819 of April 1993, and that in their intentions and operational goals, the Muslim army wanted to link up with members or, rather, to link up, territorially speaking, with the army of the 2nd Corps along the Tuzla and Kladanj axis on the one side and on the other to draw away and engage the forces of the Drina Corps, because at that time, an offensive was taking place to deblock Sarajevo. This deblocking of Sarajevo and these intentions were subjects that General Halilovic testified to. Bearing in mind all this, and especially the attacks that culminated in the course of the month of June 1995, we cannot at any event take the directives that were mentioned here, Directive 7 and 7.1, be taken as a basis for a planned operation, the planning of the operation that was called Krivaja 95. Had Directives D7 and D7.1 actually been a foundation for implementing the Krivaja 95 operation, then far earlier, perhaps already in March or April, May or June, the forces of the Drina Corps would have acted upon that directive, because, objectively speaking, they were in a far better operative and tactical position then than they were at the end of June or beginning of July 1995. Even at the beginning of June 1995, an operation was carried out, again of a limited scope, at Zeleni Jadar, the aim being to push back the forces of the 28th Division within the boundaries of the safe area. Directive 7 and 7.1 existed then too, but action was not taken pursuant to it because that was not the aim of the operation, just as the Operation Krivaja 95 was not the basis for this operation, rather, the directive was not the basis for Operation 95. The principal and only basis for the ad hoc planning and execution of Operation Krivaja 95 was to continuously inflict losses on units of the Drina Corps and the civilian population by members of the 28th Division, which this operation climaxed, as I have said, in June 1995. It should be noted that according to some data of UN Observers and the Dutch Battalion, there were artillery operations which went beyond the level of operative requirements and effective achievement of military goals as part of an offensive, and they even violated the principle of military proportionality. However, as regards the losses and casualties among Muslim civilians and soldiers, and particularly taking into consideration the level of destruction of Srebrenica, the Defence would like to submit that the operation was of limited scope and the use of these resources was limited. According to the reports of the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, dated the 6th of July, 1995, it is not possible to infer that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there were losses among civilians and the military, nor that there were large-scale destructions of civilian installations in the urban part of Srebrenica. Had such artillery devices been used to such an extent and had they been used against other targets than military ones, up to the 11th of July, there would have been far, far, far more victims; though we do not have reliable data to show that in active combat operations from the 6th to the 11th of July, the forces of the army of Republika Srpska or the Drina Corps had inflicted casualties on the enemy forces and particularly not against the civilians. I underline once again: Had artillery been used to the extent alleged, then the destruction of facilities in Srebrenica and around it would have been disastrous. However, the numerous video clips that we saw during these proceedings provided no evidence of such large-scale destruction. This may not be of great importance, but it should be noted that when the effectives of the Drina Corps reached the positions ordered, according to the order on combat operations, there was chaos within the 28th Division, and its commander, in those days, Chief of Staff, Ramiz Becirevic, was in command of the forces of the 28th Division. We know that Naser Oric was the person who was the legitimate commander of that military formation in Srebrenica; however, for certain reasons, he had abandoned the area far before the operation took place so that there is a great deal of speculation about this. As I have said, this may not be of importance for this case or for this defence, but we have heard testimony from General Halilovic about that too. There could have been a realistic -- realistically, it may have been possible to defend Srebrenica, but that is not relevant now. It should be noted in this context that it has been registered in the record, on pages 9479 to 9484, when a film was shown by the Defence in which the Muslims of Srebrenica and, in the first place, the commander of the police station, Mr. Meholjic, says that Srebrenica has been a sellout, that Srebrenica was a sellout, and this was an arrangement made at the highest state level of his country, when he charges Alija Izetbegovic and other high-level civilian and military officials for this. As I am saying, this can be no justification for everything that happened after the fall of Srebrenica, but it can be an indication, it can be a clue, showing that all this was planned who knows where and who knows by whom. God knows whether Mr. Meholjic and his story are true. Finally, his conclusion is, "Only Alija and Naser know what their arrangement was that night when they were left alone." Simultaneously with these developments and the combat operations towards the very end of Operation Krivaja 95, the President of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, and the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska decided that the forces of the Drina Corps should enter Srebrenica. This goal was achieved on the 11th of July, 1995, in the afternoon. By doing so, the Srebrenica operation was over. I say that it was completed because the goal set by the combat order to the Drina Corps Command by its commander was to narrow down the enclave to the urban area and not to capture Srebrenica. This operative goal, a decision to change that operative goal was made at some higher level. It should be said that the forces of the Drina Corps and the command of the Drina Corps, when entering Srebrenica --
