utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. When talking about important figures, officers of the army of Republika Srpska and the Drina Corps and their role in Operation Krivaja 95, the Defence has the following to say: It is quite clear that General Krstic was the chief of staff of the Drina Corps and that in that position, he was responsible for planning that operation, having received the appropriate order to do so, to prepare it, to draft a decision for the corps commander regarding the deployment of forces that would be used in the operation and to subordinate units for bringing additional units to the area of deployment and the like. The planning documents for this operation do not include a single document, nor in the combat order is there a single paragraph which could lead to the conclusion or from which it could be inferred that General Krstic, working on the basis of this order, violated the conventions of international humanitarian law or that he overstepped his competencies as prescribed by positive regulations. While the operation itself was ongoing, General Krstic did not make a single new proposal whereby the earlier decision taken by the Drina Corps Commander would be directed or changed as to the way in which the operation should be carried out or what its goals were to be. The whole operation was developed according to plan and as envisaged by the order for combat operations. True, had there been any deviation from the decision contained in the combat order, that is, had the forces of the -- it is true that the forces of the Drina Corps entered Srebrenica, but this was not something that was decided by Krstic at the forward command post, because as of the 9th of July, his immediate superior was there, that is General Zivanovic, and his second superior, the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, General Mladic. With respect to General Milenko Zivanovic, at the time of the planning, preparation, implementation, and monitoring of Operation Krivaja 95, he was the formal and factual Commander of the Drina Corps. It was his responsibility to set out the main concept of the operation, to instruct the corps staff, which was headed by General Krstic, to plan this operation, and in doing so, he proposed the engagement of forces that were necessary for this operation and how it should be carried out. General Zivanovic issued two fundamental documents for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Operation Krivaja 95, and those are for the order for active combat operation, and before that, the preparatory order number one. These are OTP Exhibits 427 and 428. It can be unequivocally alleged, on the basis of this, that during the planning, preparation, and execution of Operation Krivaja 95, General Zivanovic had the role of Commander in the Drina Corps, that he was the Commander of the Drina Corps, and that he remained in that position, according to the Prosecution until the 13th, and according to the Defence until the 20th of July. There is no trace or indication to show that General Zivanovic was absent from the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps after the 11th of July or that he was replaced by the Chief of Staff, General Krstic. The Commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, General Ratko Mladic, as the most superior commanding officer, appeared at the forward command post at Pribicevac on the 9th of July, 1995, together with General Zivanovic. He was also there on the 10th of July, and without any doubt, on the 11th of July, together with other members of the Drina Corps, both General Zivanovic and General Krstic, and together with them, he entered Srebrenica. No one can deny the legitimate right of the Commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, to be present where combat operations were ongoing, to give suggestions to the commander as to how and in what way a certain order should be implemented and carried out, to make certain corrections of any decisions, and even to issue orders to the commander as to how he should act. However, in view of the situation as it was on the 9th, 10th, and 11th of July, it is quite obvious that Mladic took over command of the units that were taking part in Operation Krivaja 95. The testimony of Witness DB clearly speaks in support of this assertion. General Krstic also testified that General Mladic took over the command of the units participating in the offensive. Both testimonies were convincingly corroborated by certain details; namely, Witness DB as well as General Krstic gave as an example the situation when Colonel Andric, who led parts of the Birac Brigade in that operation, informed that he had reached the position assigned to him by the active combat order, that General Mladic ordered him to continue the attack and to enter Srebrenica. This example of General Mladic issuing commands over the radio was also referred to by Witness DC. After units of the Drina Corps had entered Srebrenica, on the video clip that we saw here repeatedly, in the submission of the Defence, when Mladic said, "Go ahead, go ahead, on to Potocari," this is also a statement that is an order. So it shows that he was the alpha and omega of everything that was going on in that area. He was the alpha and omega to subordinate commanders and subordinate units. Neither Zivanovic nor Krstic, quite clearly, were in command at that time. Mr. President, Your Honours, this did not break the chain of command of the Drina Corps de jure. He did not, in the legal sense, take a decision or issue an order orally or in writing, and he did not say, "From now on, I am the commander of the Drina Corps." No, that is not the submission of the Defence. What the Defence wishes to say is that by his behaviour, by his verbal addresses to subordinate units and his oral orders, General Mladic in fact took over command of the forces that were, at that point in time, there in the area. Some later events linked to the 17th of July provide corroboration for this submission. In the area of the Zvornik Brigade, which should have been under the control and command of the Drina Corps, it was General Mladic who appointed an officer of the Main Staff as the Commander-in-Chief in that brigade, and by doing so, in the submission of the Defence, he was actually the one who was also in command of the Zvornik Brigade; of course, through an officer that he had designated to be the commander, and that is Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic. In this order, Exhibit 649, it says, "To command all these forces and for the execution of this task, the officer for the military police from the administration of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska army is being appointed." General Mladic also says that the command over combat operations will be performed from the command post of the battalion of the military police of the 65th Protective Regiment. The military police of the 65th Protective Regiment is, without any doubt, a unit of the Main Staff. It is headquartered in Nova Kasaba. Had the commander of the Zvornik Brigade been the real commander of his brigade at that point in time, then he would have been commanding from his own command post or forward command post. However, it is General Mladic who takes upon himself the right to deal with things in the way he sees fit, and he does so through this order. The assertion by the Prosecution, and I shall agree in part, that this was an operation which was of limited scope between the 17th and the 19th of July, it was materialised, if I could put it that way, or formalised through this act and in such a way. We do not know, except for the testimony of General Krstic himself - and the Defence has reason to believe his testimony on that point - when General Mladic, at the meeting in Bratunac, said that he takes over command in that region, but I'll come back to that question a little later on. However, pursuant to this order in which, quite obviously, the units of the 65th Protection Regiment and the Commander-in-Chief was the security officer, states that the operation was of limited scope from the 17th to the 19th of July, that is, that it had a limited time span. However, the sentence after that paragraph reads that "The order for further involvement towards Cerska will be proposed to me by Colonel Keserovic on the 19th of July, 1995." We do not know and have no proof and evidence in written form that such an order was made. But Mladic quite obviously has demonstrated his intention that if that command status of Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic were to continue after the 19th of July, without us having any proof of that, then I raise the question as to why that command status, without any proof and evidence in the form of an order, could not have existed even after the 11th, after Mladic's words were spoken in Bratunac, that that was his problem and that he would solve it. When General Mladic made the decision for entry into Srebrenica, the command of the Drina Corps quite certainly did not decide that issue, regardless of whether it was Zivanovic, Krstic -- Zivanovic or Krstic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. On the basis of OTP Exhibit 432, we can see that the document is from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. It was given to the president of Republika Srpska, addressed to him, and sent to the forward command post of the Drina Corps, to General Gvero and General Krstic personally. General Gvero was not at the forward command post at the time. From this document, we clearly see that agreement has been reached about the entrance into Srebrenica, but that agreement and who was sending out this document and to whom it was sent, so to the president of the republic, to the Main Staff, that agreement has been reached at that particular level, the level of the president of the republic and the Supreme Commander, or in other words, the Main Staff and certainly not the Drina Corps. Let me briefly dwell on that meeting of the 11th of July, which took place in the evening hours at around 2100 hours in the Bratunac Brigade. The meeting was chaired by General Mladic. Attending the meeting were, in addition to Mladic himself, General Zivanovic and Krstic, the Commanders of the units which took part in the attack on Srebrenica. According to testimonies, after a short speech pertaining to the events surrounding the entrance into Srebrenica, General Mladic ordered General Krstic to prepare and put into operation the Zepa operation. That, therefore, took place on the evening of the 11th of July. The Prosecution has attempted to state that that assertion is not correct and that it was on the 11th of July, and in that light -- that it was not on that date, and in that light, the expert witness Mr. Butler says nothing on the issue, just as if the event had never taken place. Not only did Mladic issue this order to Krstic, that is to say, mentioning the forces that took place at the Srebrenica operation and to send them to Zepa, but General Mladic also issued an order to another officer, the signals and communications commander who is directly subordinate to General Krstic and was an officer on his staff. The order that he issued to that individual at that meeting was that he should set up a forward command post and a communications centre at Zepa. Witness DB, on page 7089 of the transcript, states the following: "Mladic told Krstic that a plan should be devised straight away and the units which had taken part at Srebrenica be transferred to Zepa." He goes on to say that following this order of Mladic's, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Pandurevic reacted, and he said that that was not a good idea because they didn't know what had happened to the 28th Division and that the situation ought to be cleared up first and only then engage in a new operation. According to further testimony of DB, and this is found on page 7091 and I quote, Witness DB says: "I cannot quote or paraphrase, but generally interpreted, 'Regardless of that, everybody to Zepa.'" When he says "regardless of that" -- when he says "regardless," he's thinking of Pandurevic's operation. So regardless of Pandurevic's opposition, the combat action on Zepa should be continued. Therefore, on the 11th of July, Mladic was stating his decision to General Krstic and telling him to prepare and launch the Zepa operation. Furthermore, Witness DB goes on to say, on page 7092, the following with respect to that situation: "I think that Mladic had his own assessment of the situation on the basis of which he made the decision." So his own assessment was not to accept the proposal made by Pandurevic when he said that he didn't know what had happened with the 28th Division and that that situation ought to be settled first, and then once that had been done, to go on to the next operation. No plan, no activities whatsoever at that meeting which was attended by General Krstic himself and the other officers who had participated in the operations at Srebrenica were received. No plan was put forward. They were -- received no assignments with respect to the newly arisen situation in Potocari. A meeting with the representatives of the Dutch Battalion, the first meeting that was held before this particular meeting, was attended by General Mladic, a certain Colonel Jankovic, and General Zivanovic. It was at that meeting that General Mladic, together with General -- I'm sorry, the Colonel of the Dutch Battalion, Karremans, talked to -- talked about the withdrawal of the Dutch Battalion, of the fact that the Muslim population were to be got out, the participation of the Doctors Without Frontiers organisation, as a non-government organisation, an undertaking in the enclave. And in fact, Mladic, on that occasion addressed Karremans and asked him whether via the chief of staff of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo they could ensure buses for the transport of civilians from Srebrenica, and Karremans answered that they could reach an agreement about that. Therefore, the question of that humanitarian problem that arose, and at the meeting at which General Krstic was not present was the first time that this topic was broached. We know full well how the meetings evolved. We also know that the participants in these meetings, regardless of whether they were representatives of the civilian or military authorities of the Drina Corps, all of them except General Mladic were just mere observers. Nobody took part in the proceedings; whether because they did not want to or did not dare to is left to surmise and conjecture. General Zivanovic, though, as a participant at that first meeting, and quite obviously the problem was ensuring the means and resources for the transport of the civilian population towards Kladanj on territory under command of the BH army, therefore, General Zivanovic, the following day, that is to say, on the 12th of July, issued an order to his subordinate units to secure buses up until sometime in the afternoon on the 12th of July, up to, I think, 1630, at the stadium in Bratunac, that the buses were to be there by then. The night between the 11th and 12th of July, in Potocari, according to the testimony of witnesses appearing before this Trial Chamber, evolved relatively peacefully. It was a relatively calm night. In the course of that particular night, no units were noticed belonging to any army to upset the quiet night and to effect the refugees, which would in any way be a violation of the humanitarian law. The morning hours of the 12th of July, once again according to testimony, the morning hours were quiet too, without incident. What the witnesses have been telling us here is that the night between the 12th and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the 13th was a terrible one. From reports and testimonies by individual witnesses, members of the Dutch Battalion who followed the situation in the base itself and around the base and gained an impression of what, in fact, took place in that night between the 12th and the 13th, we arrive at the conclusion that the members - and we cannot identify them as being members of the Drina Corps - entered the base. One of the witnesses even said that he photographed nine bodies. A Prosecution witness, Bego Ademovic, testified and said that in the late afternoon of the 12th of July, he himself saw these people, the people who had entered the base and had killed 83 Muslims. The Defence does not challenge and cannot dispute the fact that that did not take place. However, the question arises of the trustworthiness of the testimony of Mr. Ademovic. Regardless of the extent to which we respect him as having been a victim, we nonetheless consider that such a large number of Muslims who had been liquidated would have been noted, would have been seen and noticed by a member of the Dutch Battalion, especially in view of the manner in which the killings were performed. We have General Krstic placed in Potocari on the 12th of July, sometime after 12.00 noon, that is to say, after the meeting in Bratunac. At that time when he was there, there was the tape that the members of UNPROFOR had positioned. Members of the opposite side, whether it was the army or the police or civilians of Republika Srpska, they were not able to cross that line that had been designated with the tape. General Krstic stayed, and this is borne out by the testimony of a Prosecution witness that we heard in closed session, he stayed there for about one hour. Together with him was his staff officer, who was responsible to him. He was subordinate to General Krstic and responsible to him; he was the intelligence officer, Svetozar Kosoric. After Krstic left towards Viogora, which is where the units were located, units of the Drina Corps which had taken part in the attack on Srebrenica because this was the position that they had reached and they had entrenched there, according to General Krstic, his staff officer went after him because he ordered him to come too, and that officer's name was Svetozar Kosoric. It is a fact that in Potocari we now see the presence of Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic as well. He was there too. However, if we go back a bit to previous events, from the beginning of the combat operation on Srebrenica, that is to say, the 6th of July or, rather, the 5th, in the afternoon, Svetozar Kosoric was together at the forward command post with General Krstic, with Colonel Vicic, Major Jevdjevic, the leader of the command, the staff command, Amovic. So all these were staff officers who were subordinate to General Krstic and to whom he was the immediate commanding officer. The fact is also that Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic, on the 11th -- was in Srebrenica on the 11th, at the entrance to Srebrenica, but we don't see him at the forward command post of Pribecevac at all. Vujadin Popovic was not there. Now, who could have brought Vujadin Popovic there and given him the order to be in Srebrenica on the 11th, 12th, maybe even later as well? It was his superior officer who could have done that, the first -- first of all, the corps commander; and secondly, he could have been issued orders by virtue of the security chain of command, the assistant commander for security or, rather, the head of the security department. At least based on the evidence put forward during the trial so far, neither Vujadin Popovic -- we did not see Vujadin Popovic at Pribicevac at all or in any way do we see his participation in that particular operation. Svetozar Kosoric was a participant at the meeting in the Fontana Hotel, together with representatives of the Dutch Battalion and the civilian authorities from Srebrenica and Bratunac, as well as the military authorities from the Drina Corps, but there simply is no evidence whatsoever to indicate any role whatsoever that that officer had or should have had and be subordinate to the chief of staff, that is, General Krstic. Together with him, after the 11th, in the personnel structure of the officer cadre taking part in the combat operations in Zepa, he is one of them. There's also Colonel Vicic as the Operations Officer; Major Jevdjevic; the Commander of the headquarters, Amovic. So if General Krstic was given the order for the planning and execution of the Zepa operation, he and his team, if I may call it that, consisting of those officers, their main concern and preoccupation was to plan, prepare, and carry out that operation. Consequently, with regard to these events that occurred on the 12th and 13th of the July, in the opinion of the Defence, General Krstic cannot be responsible for three reasons. First of all, as has been stated, he was not the commander of the Drina Corps. And even if he knew, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and he did know, that process of evacuation of the population was about to begin and that this had been agreed at the Main Staff level or, rather, decided at the Main Staff level of the army of Republika Srpska with some participation of the Dutch Battalion and international forces, to what extent they participated is something we can't go into just now, but in any event, as he was not the commander, he did not know that in the execution of that operation, unlawful acts were being committed, and this applied to him and his subordinate officers. Furthermore, as the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, he had his commander who was engaged in the area of responsibility of the corps and who had still not handed over his command to anyone. Krstic had no need nor was it his duty to supervise, carry out -- or carry out that operation. The time when this operation was carried out or, rather, the time of the events that took place between the 12th and the 13th, in the afternoon on the 13th when the population was evacuated, this was a time period which, in the submission of the Defence, Krstic was extremely busy, both he and his staff, working on the preparations and execution of the Zepa operation so that, in our opinion, he was not involved in any way in the separation of men and the evacuation of the population from Potocari. We cannot but challenge the submission of the Prosecution that Krstic had in any way directly or indirectly, either he or his subordinates, had participated in any way in the process of separation of the male population in Potocari. The time that General Krstic was there was just after 12.00, and on the video clip, buses can be seen in the background, but the actual evacuation and transport and boarding onto the buses had still not started. At that time, that unfortunate column had still not been formed, the column that would set out along the road, after which men of a certain age group were separated. The video clip that we had occasion to see showing Zoran Petrovic, Pirocanac, we see the following: In Potocari, there were no elements of the Drina Corps. The police were present, a special MUP Brigade, but not the regular police of the Zvornik Security Centre. On one of the shots, a certain member of that special unit was identified, a person nicknamed Mane. But that again is not Mane Djuric, and I think the parties are agreed on that, who was the Deputy Chief of the public security centre in Zvornik. I feel free to allege that a representative of that special unit is a certain man called Stalin, a Mr. Jevic, a personality which seems to dominate and is in the forefront. There is no evidence that Drina Corps units participated in this process of separation or that they were present in Potocari. Some witnesses whose testimonies we heard here, Prosecution witnesses, said that that night, between the 12th and the 13th of July, certain elements of the army of Republika Srpska were present, who were described by them as soldiers with dogs. In the structure of the Drina Corps, not a single unit had dogs which it would use for any purpose whatsoever. The only place - and this was confirmed by Mr. Ruez in his testimony in this courtroom and he showed us photographs - the only place where any such unit was noted was in Nova Kasaba, and that is the location of the 65th Protective Brigade of the Police Battalion -- Protective Regiment of the Police Battalion, which is not linked to the Infantry Battalion of the 65th Protective Regiment which took part in the operation on Zepa. It is a fact, and we have elaborated on this in our final brief, that the capture of Muslims occurred mostly along the Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba road and the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Those prisoners, in the submission of the Prosecution, were accommodated at the football stadium in Nova Kasaba. Various figures have been given as to the number of people rounded up there, and we simply are unable to provide any evidence to the contrary. It is also a fact that most of those prisoners were transported to Bratunac, and there, at various locations, either at the Vuk Karadzic school or in the warehouse or in the buses and trucks, they remained there during the night between the 13th and the 14th. The Prosecution alleges that the town of Bratunac was in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade and that it is the responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade to put up to the prisoners in the town or, rather, in the means of transportation that were being used. Let me say, first of all, that the town of Bratunac and its security is not the responsibility or was not the responsibility of the army. The army was at the front line. It is the civilian authorities, on the 13th of July, who were functioning in the whole town of Bratunac and Republika Srpska. The civilian police was able to perform its duties unhindered in that area. If somebody was securing those men in the sense of making sure that they do not escape, then this certainly could not have been done by members of the Bratunac Brigade, firstly, because that is not within their competence and, secondly, because, on the 13th of July, members of the Bratunac Brigade had received an order from General Krstic to search the terrain south of the Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba road, and that road remains behind them and it is not within their area of responsibility. And for that reason, they could not have been in Bratunac in the night between the 13th and the 14th. The Prosecution has not provided evidence to prove that members of the MUP were under the command of the Drina Corps. For them to be under the command of the Drina Corps, an appropriate decision would have had to be made at the level of the Minister of Internal Affairs; at least that is what the laws and regulations say with respect to the police. So the minister of the police, in coordination with the minister of the army, would have had the duty to regulate this matter, that is, the question of attachment of units. And had they been resubordinated, they could have been resubordinated only to security organs of the Main Staff, because it is at that level that the use and deployment of those units is decided. So pursuing that logic, only a step -- the resubordination of those units could be done only at that level. During the proceedings at this trial, and also the analysis provided by Mr. Butler gave the impression, in our submission, that attempts are being made to draw the Bratunac Brigade into all these developments. There is no dispute that Zoran Kovacevic and Sreten Petrovic, who were members of the Bratunac Brigade, were seen in Potocari; at least there is no dispute as far as Zoran Kovacevic is concerned being the commander of one of the battalions of the Bratunac Brigade. But his presence is on a personal basis, as an individual. There is no organised element of the Bratunac Brigade at the level of a squad or platoon or battalion or any other formation that would indicate that those elements, as organised units, were present. Zoran Kovacevic could have been in Potocari for a thousand and one reasons. First of all, he is an inhabitant of Bratunac. He had spent three years face to face with the enemy side there. In the euphoria which developed, everyone hastened to Potocari to share in the glory of victory, and his presence could be attributed to any one of a multitude of reasons, in the submission of the Defence, rather than as an officer of the Bratunac Brigade who, by his acts, contributed, as the Prosecution puts it, to the fulfilment of the plan which was adopted on the 11th of July. The Prosecution tells us that every foot soldier knew of the existence of the plan as to what should be done with those unfortunate people. Drazen Erdemovic, who testified in this Trial Chamber and who is trusted with reason, stated that on the 16th of July, when he set off for Zvornik and reached Zvornik together with his unit at Karakaj, that they were not told where they were going. This was on the 16th of July. A unit of this kind, which had been designated to take part in what it took part in, a unit whose members were selected as being special, did not know where they were going, as testified to by Erdemovic. Can the submission of the Prosecution, therefore, stand that members of the Drina Corps participated in that bloody plan? And who? When was that plan drawn up? What evidence do we have that such a plan was adopted or that the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps or even its Commander were informed of it, and that he was aware of it? Mladic's monologue, when addressing members of the Dutch Battalion and representatives of the Muslim civilian population that was repeated to survive or disappear, could that be an indication of such a plan? In the submission of the Defence, no. Mladic's verbal statements and intimidations cannot be equal to a plan and cannot, under any circumstances, include other officers of the Drina Corps in the implementation of the plan, which is one of the bases on which the Prosecution is relying for its submissions. Regardless of the -- my position regarding General Mladic, nevertheless, the Defence submits that this was just stated rhetorically as a means of intimidation. Mr. President, Your Honours, with your permission, I would suggest we adjourn for today and tomorrow morning I would complete my closing arguments by the time of the break, after which my colleague Mr. Visnjic will take over, as I had announced at the beginning.
